At first, Joan doubted the voice. She fell to her knees and prayed, "Oh, Lord, how can I, a young maiden, lead an army to save France?
Is this a true vision, or one of Satan’s lies?"
Her questions were answered by a vision of St. Catherine and St. Margaret.
They urged her to be strong and to trust in the Lord.
Joan, nevertheless, did not feel ready to lead an army, so she quietly disobeyed.
Instead of going to see Charles, she sought guidance at church and continued her normal life for four more years.
Joan’s First Battle
After a particularly vicious raid by the English in 1428, Joan finally decided to follow the directions of the Archangel Michael and lend her help to Charles’ army.
With the assistance of her family, she rode to Vaucouleurs, a nearby town, to speak with the Armagnac army captain stationed there.
Initially, he refused to listen to her, but she insisted.
To persuade the captain to allow her to meet with the heir to the throne, she predicted that his troops at Orléans would be betrayed.
Sure enough, a badly wounded soldier arrived in Vaucouleurs and confirmed Joan’s claims.
This convinced the captain, and he decided to help her reach Charles.
For eleven days, Joan, disguised in men’s clothes, traveled on horseback with an escort through dangerous Burgundian territory.
When Charles heard that an illiterate village girl was coming to deliver a message from God, he thought it might be some kind of trick.
He decided to test her.
Joan was brought into a large hall where a finely dressed man was seated on the throne.
Other nobles were standing on either side.

Without being informed which of the men was the true king, she dropped to her knees in front of Charles, who was disguised as one of his noblemen, and said, "Most Noble Lord, I was sent in the name of God to bring aid to you and your kingdom.
I can lead you to victory if you will give me an army."
Impressed by Joan’s knowledge, Charles gave her a suit of armor, a sword, and command of a small army.
She then set out for Orléans, which had been under siege by the English for over six months.
More and more people around the country joined her army when they learned that God had sent her to lead them to victory.
Once they reached Orleans, they attacked the English.
Joan stood holding the French flag, even though arrows, flaming oil, and rocks were being hurled at her and her troops.
With Joan beside them, the French soldiers were triumphant, ending the siege in nine days.
The Hope of the People
The Armagnac army’s win at Orléans gave hope to those loyal to Charles, and Joan’s army continued to grow.
When Charles met Joan to congratulate her on her victory, she told him that it was time to be crowned at Reims.
This was no easy task; Reims was located deep within enemy territory, but Joan assured Charles that it could be done.
She led her army all summer, and they succeeded in winning both Paris and Reims back from the English.
Joan was injured several times, but on each occasion, she returned to the battlefield and led her soldiers to victory.
By that winter, Joan had led France to many victories: Charles had been crowned, Paris had been liberated, and the English were retreating.
A Tragic Ending
Joan knew that if she could raise additional support and money for her army, she could finish the mission entrusted to her by the saints and push the English entirely out of France.
All winter, she sent letters to French nobles asking for support, but none came.
She was simply no longer necessary to unite the kingdom.
On May 24, 1430, Joan was defending the town of Compiegne, not far from Paris.
When the drawbridge was raised to protect the townspeople inside, Joan was stranded outside the town’s walls.
She was swiftly captured and handed over to the English for an enormous reward.
The English decided to put Joan on trial for being a witch and a heretic.
If they could prove that Joan used sorcery to achieve her victories, then they could claim that Charles had been made king by witchcraft.
The English cited the fact that Joan had worn men’s clothing as proof of her heresy.
Joan tried to explain, but the English court found her guilty and sentenced her to death.
On the day of her execution, soldiers took Joan from her prison and tied her to a stake on top of a great pile of firewood.
Joan was only nineteen years old. An English soldier took pity on her and gave her a small wooden cross.
Joan took the cross, kissed it, and exclaimed, "To those of you who have condemned me unjustly, I forgive you!
I will pray that God takes mercy on your souls."
The wood was set on fire, and as the flames engulfed her, she prayed.
Many of those involved in the trial realized that it was politically motivated.
They knew the trial was meant to discredit Charles and to get revenge for English losses during the war.
After Joan’s execution, the Cardinal of England said in great agitation: "We are ruined, for a good and holy person was burned."
The leaders who came after him agreed with the Cardinal about Joan’s innocence.
In 1449, the Pope cleared Joan of the charge of heresy, and in 1920, Joan of Arc was officially declared a saint.

episodes.title: Leonardo da Vinci: The Genius

subtitle.text: Great thinker, scientist, artist, engineer, musician, and architect─believe it or not, all of these words describe just one person!
Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian man who led a remarkable life.
He painted one of the most famous paintings in the world, invented the parachute, clock, helicopter, and tank, investigated human anatomy, and designed cathedrals and bridges.
Only one kind of person can do all these things: a genius!
But if Leonardo da Vinci was such a genius, why weren’t there parachutes and helicopters around five hundred years ago?
Well, it is through Leonardo’s notebooks that we have learned about his genius. He
recorded 13,000 pages of ideas, experiments, and observations in his many notebooks. Leonardo
da Vinci was born in 1452 in Vinci, a small town just outside of Florence, Italy. He
was the illegitimate son of a servant, Caterina, and a notary, Antonio da Vinci. After
Leonardo’s birth, his father married another woman. Leonardo
grew up happily with his father, stepmother, uncle, and grandparents. He
spent many happy, sun-filled hours in the da Vinci family’s olive orchards and vineyards. When
he was growing up, Leonardo had the habit of carrying his pencil and sketch pad with him, drawing anything that caught his eye. One
of his earliest drawings is of two ducks on a pond. The
village of Vinci overlooks the valley of the River Arno. The
countryside’s beauty is said to have deeply affected Leonardo. It
gave him an appreciation of nature that stayed with him for the rest of his life. When
he was 15 years old, Leonardo and his parents moved to Florence. Florence
was the most exciting city in all of fifteenth-century Europe because the Renaissance was starting there. Renaissance
is a French word meaning "rebirth." Before
the Renaissance, the Catholic Church had more power, money, and land than anyone else. Most people
were farmers and believed what the church told them. All art
and music was about religion. But the Renaissance changed all of this. During the
Renaissance, many advances were made in thought and culture. Ancient Greek
and Roman art, architecture, and literature were examined. The printing
press was invented. Explorers like Vasco da Gama and Christopher Columbus traveled the world. Merchants became
very rich and powerful. As a
result, they had a lot of extra money to spend on paintings, buildings, and sculptures. Leonardo couldn’t
have wished for a better time or place to begin his career. Leonardo got
his first job in Florence as an apprentice. He worked
in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, a famous painter and sculptor. Workshops like
del Verrocchio’s produced everything from paintings, sculptures, and engineering projects to decorations for parties. After three
years, Leonardo left the workshop. From 1470

until he died in 1519, Leonardo da Vinci worked as a painter, architect, sculptor, and engineer for the royal and merchant families of Italy and France, local governments, and the Catholic Church. While he
is known first and foremost as an artist, Leonardo actually spent most of his time studying science and writing his ideas and observations down in his notebooks. Unfortunately, Leonardo's interests
were so broad, and he was so often captivated by new topics, that he usually failed to finish what he started. He only completed
about six projects in his life, including the painting The Last Supper. Leonardo the Painter:
The Last Supper The Last Supper
, which Leonardo painted in 1498, is one of his masterpieces. The Last
Supper is a significant event in the Christian religion. It was
the last meal between Jesus and his apostles. Leonardo painted
The Last Supper on the wall of a dining hall in a monastery in Milan. The painting
is remarkable for two reasons. First, Jesus
and the apostles are situated very close to the viewer, creating the illusion that they and the viewers are almost in the same room. Second, the
painting depicts the most tragic moment of the Last Supper─the moment just after Jesus told everyone, "One of you will betray me." All the
apostles in the painting are reacting to his statement. There is
a lot of drama and intrigue, which is unusual for a religious painting. Leonardo the Painter:
The Mona Lisa Leonardo’s most famous
painting is the Mona Lisa , perhaps the most famous painting in the world. It hangs
in the Louvre Museum in Paris, France. The Mona
Lisa was painted in 1503, but the identity of the woman is unknown. In the
Mona Lisa , Leonardo used a new technique called sfumato , which means "smoky," to paint the outlines of his model.
Instead of painting distinct outlines, he blended the outlines into the shadows.
For example, Leonardo merged the corners of Mona Lisa’s mouth and eyes softly into the rest of her face.
This made the painting more realistic.
Some people wonder if the Mona Lisa is actually a self-portrait of Leonardo.
If Leonardo’s face is placed over Mona Lisa’s face, they seem to match!
But the greatest mystery of all is Mona Lisa’s smile─is she smiling or isn’t she?
Leonardo the Scientist: The Human Body
Like other artists of his time, such as Michelangelo and Raphael, Leonardo was interested in painting a person’s body and features accurately.
Leonardo was also interested in how the human body worked.
The best way to learn about both these things was to dissect and examine human corpses. Leonardo
drew the human body and its parts in superb detail and was the first person to correctly draw many aspects of female anatomy. He
studied muscles in great detail and drew muscles and tendons as fine threads in order to show how they attached to the bone. While
some of his drawings and observations were not accurate, many of them were. The
work of Leonardo and other scientists in the Renaissance formed the basis of modern anatomy. Leonardo
the Inventor: The Parachute, Helicopter, and Tank Leonardo
recorded his ideas for inventions in his notebooks, but he never actually built any. However,
many of them have been tested since, and they have worked! Leonardo
was the first to describe a parachute. His
drawings show a pyramid-shaped linen canopy about seven meters deep. Leonardo
also drew a helicopter made from linen, reeds, and wire. In
his plan, four men applied pressure on horizontal bars to turn a central screw. One
of Leonardo’s most famous military designs was a tank. It
was the shape of a turtle and made of wood and metal plates. It
was powered by either horses or men, and guns could be fired through narrow holes. Leonardo the
Observer: The Notebooks Leonardo’s notebooks
were just as important as his paintings. In them,
he recorded notes and illustrations on four major subjects: the science of painting, the elements of mechanics, architecture, and human anatomy. He also
included notes on his studies of botany, geology, flight, and water. It is
estimated that a third of Leonardo’s notebooks, 31 in all, survive. The notebooks are extraordinary. First, Leonardo
wrote everything backward so his writing could only be read with a mirror. Second, the
notebooks contain a large number of illustrations because Leonardo preferred pictures to writing. "The more
detail you write, the more you will confuse the reader," he said. The most
famous notebook today is the Codex Leicester , written in Milan between 1506 and 1510. It
is owned by Microsoft’s founder, Bill Gates, and his wife, Melinda Gates. Leonardo
the Inspiration: The Modern World Leonardo
da Vinci’s greatest legacy is his painting, the Mona Lisa .
It is one of the most recognizable works of art in the world and has become a modern icon.
The Mona Lisa is referenced in art and popular culture.
It has been the subject of songs, like "Mona Lisa" (1950) by Nat King Cole, and in 1919, the French artist Marcel Duchamp parodied the painting by adding a mustache. Other
artists, like Salvador Dali and Andy Warhol, have also responded to the Mona Lisa ’s popularity and used the Mona Lisa in their work.
For many years after Leonardo’s death, Leonardo was only remembered as an artist.
Eventually, his scientific observations and discoveries, recorded in his notebooks, were found.
People realized that Leonardo da Vinci was a great artist, but also a great scientist, architect, engineer, and inventor─an all-around genius.

episodes.title: The Greatest Athlete Wore a Skirt (Sometimes)

subtitle.text: Babe Didrikson was one of the greatest athletes of all time.
There was hardly a sport that Babe did not excel at, but she is best remembered for her achievements in track and field and golf from the 1930s - 1950s.
Lee Pace of Triad Golf Today Magazine stated recently that she "was every bit as formidable and dominating in her era as Tiger Woods is today."
For those who've never heard her name, 'Babe' might bring up images of Babe Ruth, the famous American baseball player.
In fact, Babe Didrikson was just as famous.
Unlike Babe Ruth, Didrikson's path to sporting achievement and earning a living from sport was difficult.
Was this because she was a woman? Yes. Was it because she refused to conform to typical ideals of femininity? Definitely.
Babe was born in 1911.
She was born 'Mildred Ella Didrikson' in Port Arthur, Texas, to parents who had recently immigrated to the United States from Norway.
She had seven brothers and sisters. Her family was working class and poor. Her father was a seaman who loved to tell stories.
Mildred Ella Didrikson got her nickname 'Babe' because she was one of the youngest in her family.
Later, the nickname reflected her prowess in baseball.
She hit so many home runs in elementary school that the boys on her team thought she was as good as Babe Ruth.
In fact, Babe found she was a 'natural' - good at every sport she tried.
Babe was born at a time when society had biased views about what women could do.
She grew up being told she should wear skirts, not play sports, and act like a 'lady.'
Babe wore a skirt occasionally but she refused to give up sports.
At school, she played with boys and wore boys' clothes so she could play baseball more easily.
While she attended Beaumont High School in Texas, Babe excelled in volleyball, tennis, baseball, basketball, and swimming.
Didrikson's best sport was basketball. Her team at Beaumont High School never lost a game.
After the teams were introduced at the beginning of a game, Babe would say, "Yup, I'm gonna beat you."
While she wasn't the most popular person on the basketball court, everyone knew that Babe was right.
After high school, Babe worked as a secretary for an insurance company in Dallas, Texas.
However, the real reason she was hired was so she could play in competitions with the company basketball team, 'the Golden Cyclones.'
Basketball was an amateur sport for women, so players needed to work in another 'everyday' job as well.
During the next three years, from 1930-1932, Didrikson led the Golden Cyclones to the national championship in 1931.
She often scored thirty or more points in an era when a team score of twenty for a game was the norm.
While she lived in Dallas, she competed in other athletic events and her interest was drawn to track and field.
She became a member of the Golden Cyclone track team.
On July 16, 1932, the sports stadium in Evanston, Illinois, was filled with sports fans.
Thousands had come to watch an exciting double event: the 1932 U.S. Olympic Trials and the women's track and field national championships.
There were over 200 women athletes.
As Didrikson entered the stadium, a few women glanced at her and smiled, but most were busy talking with their teammates.
Didrikson had no such supportive teammates. Her team, the Golden Cyclones, was represented by only one member: herself.
Earlier, when Didrikson had asked her coach whether the Cyclones would compete, he gave her a surprising answer.

"I think if you enter enough different events and give your regular performance," he told her, "you can do something that's never been done before - you can win the national championship for us all by yourself."
Babe's coach was right - she won six of eight events, broke four world records and won the championship for the Golden Cyclones!
The elated Didrikson strolled around the stadium grinning, playing her harmonica, and talking to sports reporters.
The journalists, who knew a good story when they saw one, went wild. They called her 'the super athlete' and 'the wonder girl.'
That day in Evanston made Babe Didrikson an instant legend.
Two weeks later she was part of the U.S. Olympic Team in Los Angeles, California.
She won gold and silver medals and broke world records in the javelin and hurdles. Babe Didrikson was named 'Woman Athlete of the Year.'
Babe became very popular with the American public.
Since there was no TV in those days, Babe was seen on the big screen, in the newsreels in cinemas.
She always spoke to journalists and joked around with them easily.
Sometimes she was bullied by journalists and asked rude questions about not being 'ladylike,' but she just made a joke that got everybody laughing.
Despite all the publicity, it was still difficult for Babe to make ends meet. It was the Great Depression and money and jobs were scarce.
Women could not earn money in sports so Babe joined the professional world.
She played billiards in exhibition matches, performed the harmonica in theatre shows and toured nationally with a men's baseball team.
People started to view her as a 'freak.' Women were not supposed to be doing those kinds of things.
However, Babe was earning the incredible sum of several thousand dollars a month.
In 1933, Babe Didrikson became passionately interested in golf.
She began taking lessons and worked so hard that her hands bled from holding the club so often.
By 1935, she was winning amateur tournaments.
Babe's golf style was the same as other sports she had played - she played as hard and well as she could.
She hit a golf ball with strength and power equal to men. Judging from her many victories, it worked!
When Babe started to play golf seriously, she again encountered resistance from the sports community, press and the general public.
Firstly, golf was a sport of the upper class and Babe Didrikson was working class.
Secondly, she was not a 'ladylike' golfer. In the 1920s and 30s, lady golfers were supposed to hit the ball in an elegant way.
This meant the ball didn't go very far!
Furthermore, golf was a professional sport for men but it was still considered 'unladylike' for a woman golfer to turn pro and earn money.
Babe defied convention and demanded that women golfers should get prize money too.
Didrikson, with other golfers, later organized the Ladies Professional Golf Association.
Their goal was to promote women's professional golf and increase tournament prize money. In time, they were successful.
Didrikson's golfing achievements continued through the 1940s.
She went on to win fourteen straight victories in 1947 - a feat still unequalled, even by Tiger Woods.
In her lifetime, she won a total of eighty-two golf tournaments.
In 1953, Babe was diagnosed with cancer. She continued to play golf, despite the pain, for three more years.
She was cheerful and told the press that she'd "be back on the golf course with a winning putt" soon.
Didrikson also used the press to share information about cancer, which was considered a shameful illness.
Sadly, on September 27, 1956, Babe Didrikson died at the age of 42.
When she died, Babe Didrikson was mourned by many as a great American hero.
Didrikson was especially a hero for women, because she broke down stereotypes of women.
Before and during Didrikson's lifetime, women were discouraged from being independent and pursuing their talents.
People believed women belonged at home.
Some mothers told their daughters, "Don't grow up and be like Babe Didrikson." But for many young women, Babe was a role model.
She had persevered and earned a living from sport, when it was virtually impossible for women to do so.

Furthermore, she ignored nasty comments about her sporting style - she played hard and confidently - and her personal style and life - she wore trousers and had short hair - and insisted on being forthright, encouraging and always ready for a joke.
As sportswriter Grantland Rice said, Babe Didrikson, 'the tomboy from Texas,' was "the athletic phenomenon of all time, man or woman."

episodes.title: Habitat for Humanity

subtitle.text: "What the poor need is not charity but capital, not caseworkers but coworkers.
And what the rich need is a wise, honorable, and just way of divesting themselves of their overabundance."
These words were jointly written by Millard Fuller and Clarence Jordan in a small Christian community in the state of Georgia, in the United States.
Millard Fuller and his wife, Linda, and Clarence and Florence Jordan had all left behind their well-paid jobs, fancy houses, and affluent lifestyles to live simple lives on a community farm.
Millard Fuller and Clarence Jordan dreamed of a world where all people had adequate housing.
Furthermore, they saw low-income earners not as recipients of handouts and charity, but as people who could pay their own way.
They believed people should not counsel the poor, but work alongside them.
But how? How could a few people possibly get the money, labor, and materials to build decent, simple, affordable homes?
Jordan and Fuller came up with the concept of "partnership housing."
In their vision, a family who could not afford to pay for a home would be able to work together with volunteers to build one themselves.
There would be no handouts.
The construction materials would be financed by a fund that would come from donations, fund-raising activities, and the payments of other homeowners on their loans.
In 1968, this farming community in Georgia put their ambitious plan into action.
Capital was donated from around the United States, and 42 homes were built and sold to families in need at no profit.
And thus, began the basic model for Habitat for Humanity.
In 1973, the Fuller family moved to Mbandaka, Zaire, which is now the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Their goal was to offer affordable and adequate housing for two thousand people.
After three years of hard work, they returned to the United States.
In 1976, Millard and Linda Fuller called together a group of supporters to discuss the future of their dream.
It was at this meeting that this group of dedicated people created Habitat for Humanity International.
In 1984, former United States President Jimmy Carter and his wife, Rosalynn, became involved in Habitat for Humanity International.
They led a work group to New York City to help renovate a six-story building for nineteen families.
Their personal involvement brought the organization national visibility and sparked interest in Habitat's work across the United States and internationally.
Within a few years, many local Habitat organizations, called affiliates, sprang up around the world.
Affiliates are not controlled centrally from the United States.
Rather, each affiliate acts independently and responds to local needs and objectives.
An affiliate works like this: First, a local Fund for Humanity is established.
After that, money, building materials, and building sites are donated or sold to Habitat.
Then, people living on low incomes can apply for a Habitat house.
If a family qualifies, they work side-by-side with volunteers to build their house together.
Recipients contribute at least five hundred hours of "sweat equity," which is physical work on their own home or other Habitat homes.
When their home is completed, they can buy it cheaply from Habitat, usually with a twenty-year mortgage.
Their payments are then channeled back into the local fund to build and renovate more houses.
Each affiliate also gives 10 percent of their fund to the Habitat for Humanity headquarters to fund building projects in other countries.
All Habitat for Humanity houses are built according to the same guiding principles.
Habitat houses are simple; they are modest in size but large enough for the homeowner's needs.
They are also decent; quality building materials from local sources are used, trained staff supervise construction, and houses are designed to suit the local climate and culture.
Lastly, they are affordable; the combination of volunteer labor, reasonable size, and interest-free loans makes Habitat houses affordable for low-income people around the world to buy.
Because they are designed locally, Habitat houses may look very different.
For example, Habitat houses in many African countries are built with fired clay bricks, whereas Habitat houses in the Pacific Islands are often built with wooden frames and high off the ground.
In the Philippines, many chores traditionally take place on a small porch, and so a Filipino Habitat house incorporates this custom into its design.
Who buys Habitat houses?
Ordinary people buy Habitat for Humanity houses, and they buy them for both ordinary and extraordinary reasons.
Ordinary reasons include a lack of employment opportunities, rising housing costs, or simply because the homeowners reside in a developing country.
Extraordinary reasons include natural disasters, war, famine, and illness.
The de Souza family, from Brazil, helped build their Habitat house, and they are now paying it off.
Before they bought a Habitat house, Ademar de Souza and his wife, Valderene, were paying almost half their income in rent.
When their rent went up, they were forced to move into a shack of scrap wood, cardboard, and plastic.
Of course, the de Souzas wanted something better for themselves and their seven-year-old daughter, Samara.
They applied for a Habitat house and they now live in a simple, clean, and well-built house.
In August 2001, the Jimmy Carter Work Project came to Korea and built 136 houses at 6 sites across South Korea.
More than nine thousand volunteers participated from around the world.
In Asan, 56-year-old Lee Jong Rok had been waiting all his life for a home he could call his own.
He had moved over thirty times in his life. Lee and his wife, Moon Soon Sun, had tried hard to make their housing livable.
However, their house was not properly maintained or repaired by the landlord.
Lee said, "That house was so dirty that, no matter what we did, there was no way to keep it clean."
Like all recipients of Habitat houses, Lee and his family were required to provide sweat equity─five hundred hours of building work.
Although Lee is disabled by polio and uses a wheelchair or crutches to get around, this did not stop him.
"I wanted to do more hours than required," he said. He and his family spent over eight hundred hours building Habitat houses.
Habitat for Humanity has built more than 200,000 houses around the world; 1,000,000 people now have safe decent homes of their own.
There are over 2,600 Habitat organizations in 100 countries.
The story of Habitat for Humanity is about two dreams: the dream of a safe and decent home and the dream of spending wealth in a wise and just way.
From its humble beginnings in 1976, Habitat for Humanity has proved that rich and poor can work together and make everybody's dreams come true.

episodes.title: George Washington Carver: The Plant Doctor

subtitle.text: What would it be like to be an orphan?
What would it be like to have your country discriminate against you because of the color of your skin?
What would it be like to have great dreams, but then encounter huge obstacles and not know if your dreams would come true?
One little boy knew. His name was George.
George was born a slave in Missouri in 1864, and he and his mother were owned by the Carver Farm.
One night, when he was a small baby, they were kidnapped by slave raiders.
His mother was sold and shipped away but the Carver family was able to reclaim George.
One year later, in 1865, slavery became illegal, and all of the slaves on the Carver Farm were emancipated.
But George stayed with the Carvers, who treated him like family.
They gave him their name, and he became known as George Washington Carver.
The Carvers were kind and encouraged the young boy to learn and realize his potential.
While he was living with them, Mrs. Carver taught him to read and write, and Mr. Carver taught him about plants and basic agriculture.
The young Carver was a very fast learner.
The only books he owned were a dictionary and a Bible, and he read them all the time.
He learned to love plants by watching and painting pictures of them as they changed throughout the year.
In fact, he became so skilled in his understanding of the biology of plants that the neighbors brought their sick plants to him and called him "the Plant Doctor."
As much as he loved the farm, Carver only stayed there until he was about 11 years old.
What he wanted more than anything was to study at a university. In order to do this, he first had to attend high school.
Tragically, the schools in his town refused to teach him because he was black.
Slavery had been abolished for ten years, but many white people were still racist, and segregation still existed in many places in the southern United States.
For the next seven years, Carver moved around, eventually graduating from high school in Minnesota.
In 1885, he was accepted to Highland University in Kansas.
He was thrilled! But as soon as the school saw his skin color, the school administrators forced him to leave.
They refused to teach a black man.
One day, Carver received a letter from Simpson College in the state of Iowa; it was an invitation to become their first black student.
Carver was jubilant to see his dream come true.
So, at the age of 25, he began his study of art at the college and worked as a farmhand to support himself.
Carver was a wonderful painter, but he missed working with plants.
So he transferred from Simpson College to nearby Iowa State College to study agriculture.
In 1896, Carver graduated from Iowa State College with a master's degree in science.
Booker T. Washington, a respected African American political leader and the founder of the Tuskegee Institute, invited him to teach there.
Carver happily accepted the position.
During his time at Tuskegee, Carver became a world-famous scientist.
He discovered that planting cotton damaged and exhausted the nutrients in the soil, while planting peanuts and sweet potatoes replenished them.
But, the farmers were dependent on cotton, and no one wanted to plant acres and acres of peanuts or sweet potatoes.
Who would want so much of these crops? So Carver worked hard to solve that problem.
Carver was convinced that he could teach the farmers of the South to enrich their soil.
Over the next 44 years, Carver experimented with peanuts and sweet potatoes.
He discovered a hundred new ways to use sweet potatoes, to make vinegar, flour, syrup, coffee, glue, alcohol, soap, and many other everyday products.
What was even more amazing was that he discovered three hundred applications for peanuts!
Peanuts could be used to make cheese, candy, shampoo, ink, linoleum, paper, and even medicine.

To prove the importance of peanuts, Carver invited some very famous people over for dinner to discuss his discoveries; politicians, academics, leaders of industry, and other scientists accepted the invitation.
He served a mouthwatering meal of soup, chicken casserole, bread, salad, coffee, cake, and ice cream.
After dinner, Carver got up to give a speech. "Every dish I have served tonight included peanuts in some form," he said.
The guests were astounded and applauded his work.
In 1921, Carver made a speech to the U.S. Congress about how American-grown peanuts could help the South, and Congress agreed by imposing a tax on imported peanuts.
To this day, many people credit Carver with saving the South's way of life.
With all his monumental discoveries, Carver could have received international acclaim and great wealth.
But George refused to accept money for his inventions.
He believed God had given him his ideas, so it would have been wrong to profit financially from them.
Instead, he continued to teach and inspire his students.
"I am trying to get black Americans to understand that their color does not inhibit them as much as they might think," he once said.
Carver also traveled throughout the South, helping black and white farmers understand how to take care of their land and how to diversify their crops.
Once again, he was the "Plant Doctor" that farmers respected.
"I believe God's gifts will transform our race in the eyes of the world," he would tell the black farmers.
Carver knew that helping black people become better farmers would help them earn respect as Americans.
As Carver's reputation grew, he met with three U.S. presidents.
The crown prince of Sweden also once spent three weeks studying with him.
Despite his busy career, Carver also continued to create art.
Seventy-one of his paintings made from vegetables and clay pigments were called masterpieces and showcased in an art exhibit in 1941.
Despite his fame and accomplishments, his favorite place to be was in his laboratory doing experiments.
And that is where he stayed, working every day until he died on January 5, 1943, at the age of 79.
Since he had no family, in his will, he left all his earnings to the Tuskegee Institute to help future scientists.
"It is not the style of clothes one wears," wrote Carver, "neither the kind of automobile one drives, nor the amount of money one has in the bank that counts.
These mean nothing. It is simply service that measures success."
Because of his service to others, George Washington Carver earned the respect of an entire nation.
"He could have added fortune to fame, but caring for neither,
he found happiness and honor in being helpful to the world."
- Epitaph on George Washington Carver's grave </center>
